questions.why: Floating 60%×2,500 = 1,500; +1.5% = Rs 22.5 crore — straight arithmetic on the floating base only.

questions.stem: Silverleaf's treasury: borrowings Rs 2,500 crore, 60% floating at MCLR-linked rates (currently 8.8%), 40% fixed at 9.2% with 7 years left; revenue growth 9% p.a.; management fears +150 bps but expects a cut in two years.

questions.q: If instead rates rise +50 bps and the company swaps 50% of the floating book to fixed at 9.0%, year-1 interest cost versus the pre-shock baseline is approximately:
questions.why: Hedged half (750 Cr) locked at 9.0 vs old 8.8 ⇒ +1.5 Cr; unhedged half floats 8.8→9.3 ⇒ +3.75 Cr; total +5.25 Cr (vs +7.5 Cr fully unhedged). The swap cut the bill, not erased it.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — this topic stays active in ICAI question-setting Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

questions.q: The two-year rate-cut expectation argues for:
o: Keep more floating or buy a floor/cap ladder — a payer swaption to switch to fixed if the expected cut fails — options fit a two-sided view
questions.why: When a favourable move is expected but not certain: cap (rate-rise insurance) or payer swaption (right to fix later); locking fixed today forfeits the expected cut.

questions.q: A 3-year 10% annual-coupon bond at par has modified duration (approx, Macaulay ≈ 2.78; yield 10%):
questions.why: ModDur = MacDur/(1+y) = 2.78/1.10 ≈ 2.53. The trap is answering Macaulay directly.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: HIGH likelihood for Nov 2026 — duration-with-1+y divisor is a signature trap Prediction is study guidance, not an ICAI statement.

mem.tip: Duration shrinks when you divide by (1 + yield) — modified is the one that forecasts price.

questions.q: Immunisation of a bank's portfolio requires approximately:
o: Duration of assets = duration of liabilities (and adequate convexity/size matching)
questions.why: Classic Redington/DGAP: match durations (and convexity ≥), so net worth is insensitive to small parallel rate moves.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — the matching-conditions list AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Immunisation is balance on the seesaw: equal durations, never equal maturities.

questions.q: Hedging a jet fuel position with crude futures exposes the manager to:
o: Basis risk — the difference between spot and futures prices may move against
questions.why: Cross-hedges leave BASIS (spot − futures) movement as residual risk; quality/location/tenor mismatches create it.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — the residual-risk naming on cross hedges AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: No hedge is a perfect suit — the basis is how it fits.

questions.q: For the same duration, a higher-convexity bond benefits an investor when:
o: Rates move sharply in EITHER direction
questions.why: Convexity = positive curvature: price rise for rate fall > price fall for rate rise — valuable under large moves.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — the curvature-vs-duration pairing AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Duration predicts the tangent; convexity is the discount for being wrong in both directions.

questions.q: A payer swaption gives the holder the right to:
o: Enter the swap paying fixed (if it's a receiver of fixed? payer = pays fixed under the swap)
questions.why: Payer swaption → right to enter a swap as fixed-payer (benefits when rates rise → swap value +); receiver → fixed-receiver.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — naming-perspective convention Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Payer/receiver is who you become inside the swap, not what you pay the seller.

questions.q: A borrower exposed to rising rates should buy:
o: A cap on the reference rate (pay the premium, receive when rates exceed strike)
questions.why: Cap = series of call options on the rate (receipts when reference > strike) — insures a floating-rate payer's cost; floor for a lender.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — cap-floor-buyer mapping AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Borrowers buy ceilings; lenders buy floors — the premium is the insurance card.

questions.why: %ΔP ≈ −5.5 × 0.5% = -2.75%. Rates up, prices down — magnitude only from duration; convexity would improve it slightly.

questions.q: An institution's assets have duration 5.5 and liabilities 2.0, funded by them. Rates rise 100 bps; equity value roughly:
o: Falls ~3.5% of assets (duration gap × Δy × assets)
questions.why: ΔEquity ≈ −(D_A − D_L×L/A)×Δy×A; with 1:1 funding the gap 3.5 × 1% of the asset base is destroyed — that is the savings-and-thrift story in one formula.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — equity = the lever of the duration mismatch AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Same boat, unequal clocks: the long side sinks deeper.

questions.q: For the same duration and rate move, a bond with greater convexity:
o: Loses more on yield rises and gains less on falls
Gains MORE on yield falls than it loses on equal yield rises
Is riskier in both directions identically
questions.why: Convexity is the second-order bonus: price-yield curves bow toward the holder — bigger gains on rallies, smaller losses on sells; portfolios long optionality (callable short ≠) own this; deep discount/MBS cases shift the sign — quote the sign of convexity, never 'curvature' blindly.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — positive convexity is the market paying you for patience Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: A curved ladder is kinder climbing than falling.
